newsitem.title: UK: High-profile biotech firm sees no products for 5 years.
newsitem.headline: High-profile biotech firm sees no products for 5 years.

text.p: PPL Therapeutics Plc, which stunned the world by helping to clone a sheep, will take five years to put any biotechnology product on the market, and investors can expect more near-term losses, its director said Monday.
But the British company said it held patents on its controversial cloning techniques and potential new products that should keep investors interested.
Managing Director Ron James said PPL would continue to concentrate on animals such as sheep, cattle, rabbits and pigs that have been genetically engineered to produce human proteins.
But James warned the technology was still clumsy and unreliable, although he was confident this would improve.
Asked how long before PPL had a cloning or other biotechnology product on the market, James answered, "It's at least five years away."

Researchers, led by embryologist Dr. Ian Wilmut at the Roslin Institute in Edinburgh, Scotland, announced late last month they had created a lamb using DNA from an adult sheep. PPL sponsored the research and has applied for patents.

Announcing its first annual results since the company was listed on the stock market last year, PPL on Monday reported a pretax loss of 6.2 million British pounds ($9.9 million). Revenues hit 2.5 million pounds ($4 million).

"I think we might see this level of turnover continue," said PPL Finance Director Richard Cruse. "We will also expect to see the 8.25 million sterling ($13.2 million) (in development costs) increase again."

Revenues fell from 4 million pounds ($6.4 million) when Bayer AG withdrew its support for PPL's lead product, alpha anti-trypsin (AAT), a human protein produced in milk from genetically engineered sheep.

AAT is about to undergo Phase II clinical trials for use in treating cystic fibrosis. In the United States, Phase II trials are generally the first test of a drug on humans to determine whether they work and precede the final Phase III test that comes before a drug is submitted for regulatory approval.

James said PPL hoped to find a partner for AAT by the middle of next year. "Our plan here is to get a partner on board at the end of the Phase II trial," he said. "We obviously need to start talking to them before then and we are talking to potential partners now."
Commercial arrangements are under way for marketing various products with Novo Nordisk A/S of Denmark, Wyeth Laboratories Ltd. and Euro Pharma Co.
James said product development was on schedule.

Four new potential products showed hope, he added. One was a calcitonin peptide -- produced in milk by genetically engineered rabbits -- which might be of use in treating osteoporosis and Paget's Disease.

Another product PPL has negotiated the rights for was EC SOD (extracellular super oxide dismutase), for which James saw potential in treating Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) and in preserving human organs for transplant.
There is also a novel anti-protease -- a chemical that works against elastase, an enzyme implicated in inflammation -- and of possible use in ARDS, wound healing and cystic fibrosis.

The fourth was a range of novel collagen compounds. Collagen holds the body together and can be used in tissue modelling. James said PPL could use its genetic engineering techniques to tailor collagens for researchers.
